_note: Every in-game fact with its source. Add new facts here at the same time as you add them to the game.

facts.text: Moon gravity is about 1/6 of Earth's, so you jump high and fall slowly.
facts.value: 1.62 m/s² (Earth 9.81 m/s²)

facts.text: An astronaut breathes in about 0.9 kg of oxygen every day.
facts.value: 0.895 kg per crewmember per day (BVAD Table 3-31, p. 58)

facts.text: Working outside in a spacesuit is hard work, so you use oxygen about 2 times faster.
facts.value: 0.086 kg per hour on a spacewalk (BVAD Table 4-70, p. 135) vs 0.037 kg per hour inside

facts.text: Hard work outside in a spacesuit burns more food energy — about 2 times more per hour.
facts.value: 1.062 MJ per hour on a spacewalk (BVAD Table 4-70, p. 135) vs 12.778 MJ per day = 0.53 MJ per hour normally (Table 3-31, p. 58)

facts.text: An astronaut eats about 0.8 kg of food per day (not counting the water in it).
facts.value: 0.800 kg dry mass per crewmember per day (BVAD Table 3-31, p. 58)

facts.text: At the Moon's south pole the Sun stays low and slowly circles the sky. In real life one trip around takes about 29.5 days.
facts.value: Synodic period 29.53 days

facts.text: The Moon has almost no air, so the sky is black even when the Sun is up, and shadows are sharp.
facts.value: Surface pressure about 3 × 10⁻¹⁵ bar

facts.text: Electrolysis uses electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen.
facts.value: 2 H₂O → 2 H₂ + O₂ (the ISS Oxygen Generation Assembly does this to make breathing oxygen)

facts.text: Space greenhouses like NASA's Veggie light plants with red and blue LEDs, which is why the greenhouse glows pink-purple.
facts.value: Veggie tests different red:blue light ratios (VEG-04, 2019)

facts.text: At the south pole the Sun is always low, so NASA is testing tall vertical solar arrays that turn to follow it.
facts.value: NASA Vertical Solar Array Technology (VSAT) project

facts.text: Every water molecule (H₂O) has 1 oxygen atom and 2 hydrogen atoms, so splitting water gives twice as much hydrogen gas as oxygen gas.
facts.value: 2 H₂O → 2 H₂ + O₂; H₂ at the negative electrode, O₂ at the positive; 1.125 kg water per kg O₂

facts.text: Splitting water takes at least about 5 kWh of energy for every kg of oxygen; real machines need more.
facts.value: ΔfH°(H₂O, l) = −285.83 kJ/mol × 62.5 mol/kg O₂ = 17.9 MJ ≈ 4.96 kWh per kg O₂ (minimum)

facts.text: The Space Station's oxygen machine makes oxygen by electrolysis.
facts.value: 2.3–9.2 kg O₂ per day selectable (NTRS 20080036243); 5.4 kg/day nominal (NTRS 20180006335)

facts.text: On the Space Station, a Sabatier reactor joins hydrogen with the CO₂ astronauts breathe out to make water; the methane it also makes is let out into space.
facts.value: CO₂ + 4 H₂ → CH₄ + 2 H₂O

facts.text: Splitting salt water makes chlorine gas at the + side instead of oxygen, and chlorine is poisonous.
facts.value: 2 Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2 e⁻ at the positive electrode

facts.text: Craters near the Moon's south pole that never get sunlight hold water ice.
facts.value: LRO LEND data: ice in permanently shadowed regions near the south pole

facts.text: Gravity is the same inside the base: still about 1/6 of Earth’s.
facts.value: 1.62 m/s² on the lunar surface; walls and air do not change it

facts.text: NASA’s Astrobee robots fly inside the Space Station using electric fans; they cannot work outside.
facts.value: Fan (impeller) propulsion, ISS interior only

facts.text: On the airless Moon, rovers roll on wheels; the Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle used wire-mesh wheels.
facts.value: LRV wire-mesh wheels (NASA Glenn TM)

facts.text: Plants mainly use red and blue light to grow, so grow lights look pink.
facts.value: NASA Veggie VEG-04 red:blue light study

facts.text: Sunlight is made of tiny packets of energy called photons. When a solar cell absorbs one, it knocks an electron loose.
facts.value: Photovoltaic effect (Solar Fix lesson, step 1)

facts.text: A solar cell pushes loose electrons to one side like a battery; connect a wire and they flow one way round the circuit: direct current (DC).
facts.value: Solar Fix lesson, step 2; the cell works like a diode (one-way gate)

facts.text: A solar cell is built like a diode, which lets current flow in only one direction.
facts.value: Solar Fix lesson, Go deeper card

facts.text: Solar cells are joined in chains (in series). A cell that makes no electricity holds back its whole chain.
facts.value: 'shading one cell causes the current in the string of cells to fall to the level of the shaded cell' (Solar Fix lesson, step 3)

facts.text: A radio message takes about 1.3 seconds to travel between the Moon and Earth, because nothing goes faster than light.
facts.value: 384,400 km ÷ 299,792.458 km/s = 1.28 s one way (supply terminal)
